understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call fear of what might happen, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: From boiling inside and feeling trapped by the children, to speaking the true thing and finding the courage to act without letting the family become your only reason to stay.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the betrayal and the anger, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the harm deepens only if you let their word replace what you know in your body.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what you know in your body cannot be made smaller by what they say.
week_beats.act: You try speaking the true thing to her, gently and firmly, and find the courage the moment asks for.
week_beats.story: A man whose trust was broken questions his wife and finds the footing to act without letting the family become his prison.

understanding.core_struggle: He found messages on his wife's phone, was told it was only talking, and now feels betrayed, boiling inside, and trapped by the children.
understanding.mirror: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.
understanding.insight: None of this is your fault. You deserve to feel safe, and you don't have to face it alone.

queries.hook: Living in fear in your own home, hurt by someone who should protect you, and feeling there is no one to turn to.
queries.diagnose: Being hurt by someone is never your fault; the one who harms carries that wrong, and silence kept for the sake of peace only lets harm grow.
queries.steady: What is being done to you is not your fault and not your burden to carry; your safety and your worth matter.
queries.act: Protect yourself and those who depend on you; speak the truth to someone you trust, and find the courage to seek help.
queries.story: A man whose trust was broken by his own, who questioned her openly, and found the footing to act without letting the family become his prison.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse.sanskrit: नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते । स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात् ॥
verse.line: No sincere effort here is ever wasted. Even a little of it shields you from great fear.
verse.translation: On this path no effort is lost and no harm results. Even a little of this practice protects one from great fear.

words.en: here no stepping back, no destruction

verse.why: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

prasang.title: The yoga of action
prasang.summary: Krishna teaches the yoga of action: work wholeheartedly, give up clinging to outcomes, stay even in success and failure, and keep a single steady purpose.
prasang.lesson: Do the work fully; let go of owning the result.

verse.for_you: What is real in you cannot be taken or lost; only what changes can be taken, and you are more than what changes.

verse.speaker: Vishnu
verse.setting: Vishnu explains to the frightened gods where fear comes from.
verse.sanskrit: दीनताजं भयं माने गुणे खलभयं खलु । भयं निन्दकजं शक्तौ विद्यायां वादिनं भयम् ॥
verse.line: Honour fears disgrace, virtue fears the wicked, power fears critics, learning fears debate. Every gain brings a fear.
verse.translation: In honour lies the fear of being brought low; in virtue, the fear of the wicked; in power, the fear of critics; in learning, the fear of rival debaters.
verse.why: Every gain brings its own fear; holding things lightly is the way out.

prasang.title: Vishnu on where fear comes from
prasang.summary: The frightened gods ask Vishnu how to become fearless. He explains that every possession carries its own fear (the body fears age, wealth fears thieves, power fears critics) and that only dispassion is free of fear; then he restates Bhagavad Gita 2.14-15 on enduring pleasure and pain.
prasang.lesson: Every gain brings its own fear; holding things lightly is the way out.

verse.meaning: The gods are frightened and ask Vishnu how to become fearless. He tells them that every possession carries its own fear. Honour fears disgrace, virtue fears the wicked, power fears critics, and learning fears debate. Every gain brings a fear with it. The way out is not to drop everything, but to hold your gains lightly, without letting them own your peace.
verse.for_you: The messages on the phone are a gain you did not ask for, and now they bring a fear of what might happen. But the fear is not the messages. It is the weight you give them.
verse.try_today: Notice when your body tightens around a thought about what might happen, and let the thought pass without following it.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own knowledge while the future stays unwritten.
asks: How do I tell letting go from ignoring what I know?
What gain is bringing this fear into my house?
Can I hold the truth without letting it burn me up?

verse.speaker: Lakshman
verse.setting: After Sita is taken, Lakshman comforts Ram, who is lost in grief.
verse.sanskrit: आश्वसिही नरश्रेष्ठ प्राणिनः कस्य नापदः। संस्पृशन्त्यग्निवद् राजन् क्षणेन व्यपयान्ति च॥
verse.line: Take heart. Trouble touches everyone; it flares up like fire and passes.
verse.translation: Take heart, best of men. Which living being does trouble not touch? Troubles strike like fire, king, and pass in a moment.
verse.why: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

prasang.title: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.story_hook: He came back to the hut calling her name, and no one answered.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

verse.meaning: Lakshman speaks to Ram in the Aranya Kanda after Sita has been taken. Ram is broken. He has searched the empty hut, asked the trees and the animals, and finally he has fallen into a rage, ready to burn the whole world down. Lakshman tells him to take heart. He says that no living being is spared trouble. It strikes like fire, and then it passes. The verse does not ask Ram to stop feeling. It asks him to hold that the fire is not his alone, and that it will not last forever.
verse.for_you: You are boiling inside because you found those messages and she told you it was only talking. That betrayal is real and it hurts. Lakshman tells Ram that trouble touches everyone and then passes. The fire you feel is not yours alone, and it will not last forever.
verse.scene_line: You are in the empty hut, asking the trees, and then breaking down in rage.
asks: How do I tell the fire passing from the fire burning?
How do I stop the rage without letting it destroy everything?

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: पातितोऽपि कराघातैरुत्पतत्येव कन्दुकः । प्रायेण साधुवृत्तनामस्थायिन्यो विपत्तयः ॥
verse.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
verse.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.misuse: Not a promise that suffering is always short, or that people who suffer long did something wrong.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari writes this for the reader who has been knocked down. He is not talking about a game. He is talking about a life that has been knocked off its feet. He says the ball does not stay on the ground. It flies right back up. He says the misfortunes of those who keep walking the right path do not last. This is not a promise that the pain will vanish tomorrow. It is a statement about the nature of a steady path.
verse.for_you: You know what happened. You do not need to make it smaller because they said it was only talking. The path you are on is the one where you see clearly and you stay. The setback is not your life.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own room, holding what you know.
asks: How do I know if I am still on the right path?
What does the right path look like for me right now?
Can I trust that the path itself will hold me?

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: त्रीण्येव तु पदान्याहुः सतां वृत्तमनुस्मरन् / न चैव द्रुह्येद्दद्याच्च सत्यं चैव सदा वदेत्
verse.line: Good people walk three steps: never betray anyone, give generously, and always tell the truth.
verse.translation: Recalling the conduct of the good, the wise name just three steps: never betray anyone, give, and always speak the truth.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

prasang.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.meaning: In the city of Mithila, a wise meat-seller named Dharmavyadha speaks to a proud Brahmin ascetic named Kaushika. The ascetic has come to learn what real goodness is, and the butcher tells him that the wise walk three steps. They never betray anyone, they give generously, and they always tell the truth. The butcher shows the ascetic that wisdom is not in the forest, but in the honest work of ordinary life, and that caring for your parents is part of this path.
verse.for_you: Do what you can today, take refuge in what does not change, and meet each moment with courage instead of rehearsing the worst.
verse.try_today: State one true thing about the situation out loud, to yourself or to her.
verse.scene_line: You stand in your own kitchen, holding the evidence of a betrayal, and you could choose the third step.
asks: How do I speak the truth without making the children suffer more?
Can I be firm and still stay in this house?

verse.speaker: Beings of the sky
verse.setting: Having outwitted two monsters mid-flight, Hanuman is praised by those watching from the sky.
verse.sanskrit: यस्य त्वेतानि चत्वारि वानरेन्द्र यथा तव। धृतिर्दृष्टिर्मतिर्दाक्ष्य स कर्मसु न सीदति ॥
verse.line: Steadiness, clear sight, good judgement and skill. With these four, you won't sink at work.
verse.translation: Whoever has these four, as you do, chief of monkeys, never sinks in his work: steadiness, clear sight, judgement and skill.
verse.why: Gratitude and focus can go together; know when to be big and when to be small.

prasang.title: Hanuman's leap
prasang.summary: Hanuman leaps across the ocean. A mountain rises to repay an old kindness by offering rest; he thanks it but keeps his promise not to stop. He outwits Surasa by shrinking small and defeats Simhika, and the watching beings praise his steadiness, sight, judgement and skill.
prasang.story_hook: Halfway across the ocean, a golden mountain rose out of the water and offered him a place to rest.
prasang.lesson: Gratitude and focus can go together; know when to be big and when to be small.

verse.for_you: Most of what you fear hasn't happened. Your mind keeps living it in advance, again and again.

story.title: Bharata wrongly blamed
story.story_hook: He had done nothing, and the one person whose good opinion he needed was sure he had done it all.
story.summary: Bharata turns on his mother in fury. Then Ram's grieving mother assumes he plotted it all, and her words cut him like a needle in a wound. He falls at her feet and swears his innocence until she believes him.
story.lesson: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

anchor.speaker: Bharata
anchor.setting: Grieving Kausalya accuses Bharata of plotting Ram's exile; he knew nothing of it.
anchor.sanskrit: आर्ये कस्मादजानन्तं गर्हसे मामकल्मषम्। विपुलां च मम प्रीतिं स्थितां जानासि राघवे॥
anchor.line: Why blame me, who knew nothing? You know what I feel for him.
anchor.translation: Noble lady, why do you blame me, who knew nothing and did nothing wrong? You know how deep my love for Ram is.
anchor.why: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

prasang.title: Bharata wrongly blamed
prasang.summary: Bharata turns on his mother in fury. Then Ram's grieving mother assumes he plotted it all, and her words cut him like a needle in a wound. He falls at her feet and swears his innocence until she believes him.
prasang.story_hook: He had done nothing, and the one person whose good opinion he needed was sure he had done it all.
prasang.lesson: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

story.hook_title: Bharata had done nothing, and Kausalya was sure he had done it all
story.teaser: Bharata had done nothing, and Kausalya was sure he had done it all
story.for_you: Bharata stood in the court where his mother had accused him, and the hurt came not from the charge but from the source. You are standing in a similar court now.
asks: How do I speak the truth without breaking the children's world?
Can my truth be spoken without making the house smaller?
